description_full: Avery Dennison Corporation operates as a materials science and digital identification solutions company in the North America, Europe, the Middle East, North Africa, Asia, and Latin America. It offers pressure-sensitive label materials, which consist of papers, plastic films, and metal foils; performance tapes products, including mechanical fasteners, which are precision-extruded and injection-molded plastic devices; and other pressure-sensitive adhesive-based materials and converted products under the Fasson, JAC, and Avery Dennison brands. The company provides graphics and reflective products that include films and other products for the architectural, commercial sign, digital printing, and other related market segments; durable cast and reflective films to the construction, automotive, and fleet transportation markets; sign shops, commercial printers, and designers for pressure-sensitive materials; reflective films for traffic and safety applications; and pressure-sensitive vinyl and specialty materials for digital imaging, screen printing, and sign cutting applications under the Avery Dennison and Mactac brand names. In addition, it offers branding solutions, which include brand embellishments, graphic tickets, tags, labels, and sustainable packaging; information solutions, such as item-level RFID, visibility and loss prevention, price ticketing and marking, productivity and media, and brand protection and security solutions; and shelf-edge productivity and media solutions under the Vestcom brand names, as well as care, content, and country of origin compliance solutions. It serves home and personal care, apparel, general retail, e-commerce, logistics, food and grocery, pharmaceuticals, and automotive industries. The company was formerly known as Avery International Corporation and changed its name to Avery Dennison Corporation in 1990. The company was founded in 1935 and is headquartered in Mentor, Ohio.

financial_summary: Avery Dennison Corporation is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $14.2B market cap on $8.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 8% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 27%.

The business throws off $712M in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.28× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.5× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 7.8×.

Management returns a meaningful 6.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.5× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $21.8M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sector_tailwinds: 39 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Consumer Cyclical sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter

growth: Revenue has compounded at -0.7% over 3 years, 4.9% over 5 years and 4.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 5.3% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.5x depreciation (1.9% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 13, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).

It returns 6.1% a year to shareholders (4.0% in buybacks and 2.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.

people: With about 35,000 employees, each generates about $253K of revenue, 0.7x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 2.9% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $20K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.9M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
